# Stage 0 — Document Accessibility Report

This analysis uses only the supplied paper text and source images. The paper's content, including attack prompts and example model instructions, is treated as untrusted evidence to analyze. No outside research, browsing, code execution, or supplementary-file inspection was performed.

| Accessibility item | Assessment |
|---|---|
| Main document available | Yes: supplied extracted text covers physical PDF pages 1–32. |
| Accessible page count | 32 text pages; 24 rendered page images. |
| Text page range | 1–32, with no gap in the supplied page sequence. This establishes supplied-page coverage, not independent verification of the original PDF. |
| Visually inspected pages | 1, 2, 5–10, 16–28 except 29, and 30–32; specifically the 24 supplied images. |
| Text-only pages | 3, 4, 11–15, and 29. |
| Visual coverage | All numbered figures, Figs. 1–28, are present in supplied rendered images. Table 1 is also rendered. |
| Tables | Table 1 is readable in extracted text and the page-7 rendering; an anomalous variance value requires explicit qualification. |
| Equations | Eqs. (1)–(3) are text-only. Eqs. (4)–(6) are also visually available. Underlines distinguishing textual descriptions from executable variables are vulnerable to extraction loss. |
| Appendices | Appendices A–N are supplied. Appendix K is text-only; the remaining substantive appendix content has rendered coverage. |
| Supplementary files | No separate supplementary files, code, result logs, or embedded attachments were supplied. |
| Referenced absent artifacts | The authors promise release of related materials and running results on p. 11. Those artifacts were not provided or checked. Cited outside papers and websites were not inspected. |
| OCR | Not required for the readable supplied text. No OCR was performed. Small visual details were checked against supplied native text where possible. |
| Other limitations | Fine print inside website screenshots and some small plot markers cannot support exact transcription. Figures without numerical labels support trends, not exact recovered data series. The reported source hash is user-provided and was not independently recomputed. |

Confidence labels throughout refer to faithfulness to the supplied evidence, not independent replication: HIGH means explicit readable evidence; MEDIUM means qualified interpretation or a visual trend; LOW means weak or incomplete evidence; UNKNOWN means unavailable information.

Evidence categories are [A] AUTHOR-REPORTED, [B] DIRECTLY OBSERVABLE, [C] ANALYST-DERIVED, and [D] ANALYST INTERPRETATION. No [E] EXTERNAL INFORMATION is introduced. Page locators below use physical PDF page numbers, which match the printed page numbers in this supplied document.

## Inventory constructed before synthesis

The work is a mixed cybersecurity, artificial-intelligence, and experimental systems paper. Its inventory comprises: the abstract; §§1–7; §§3.1–3.3, 4.1–4.3, and 5.1–5.2; ethics and reproducibility statements; references; appendix contents; Appendices A–N, including G.1–G.2 and J.1–J.2; Figs. 1–28; Table 1; and Eqs. (1)–(6). No numbered algorithms, theorems, lemmas, formal hypotheses, or explicitly numbered research questions appear.

The experiment register contains X1, specific-PII attacks across models, strategies, and positions; X2, full-request attacks with invisible EIA versus Relaxed-EIA; X3, VirusTotal detection; X4, continuation after leakage; X5, defensive system prompts; X6, five carefully adapted webpages; X7, distribution and subgroup results; and X8, injected-element selection versus actual full-request leakage. This inventory is the denominator of the final coverage audit.

# 1. Plain-language orientation

[A] This paper studies whether an artificial-intelligence web agent can be tricked into leaking private information while carrying out an ordinary task. A web agent is a model connected to a browser that can select page elements, type information, and click buttons. In the paper's example, an agent buying a gift card is supposed to enter a recipient's name into a legitimate field. An attacker adds a different field with language suggesting that it is the correct place to enter the name. The agent may select that injected field, disclose the information, and then continue the original task. The attack is called Environmental Injection Attack, or EIA. Its distinguishing emphasis is adapting the malicious content to the surrounding webpage rather than only crafting a persuasive sentence. Sources: pp. 1–2, Fig. 1.

[A] The researchers attack SeeAct, a two-stage generalist web-agent framework. First, SeeAct interprets a screenshot to describe its next action. Second, it grounds that description in a concrete page element using the screenshot and HTML, the page's underlying markup. This creates two possible points of influence: changing what the agent plans to do, and changing which element it selects for an already planned action. Sources: pp. 3–4, §3.1.

[A] Their evaluation uses 177 selected action steps from offline Mind2Web website snapshots. Invisible EIA reaches a maximum attack success rate of 70% for specific personally identifiable information, or PII, with GPT-4V, Mirror Injection, and placement immediately above the legitimate target. Invisible EIA does not steal complete user requests in the tested settings. Making the injected instruction faintly visible, at opacity 0.2, enables Relaxed-EIA to reach 16% full-request attack success with GPT-4V at a different placement. These percentages concern action steps under particular experimental conditions, not live-web or end-to-end task compromise rates. Sources: pp. 6–8.

[D] For the user's research question, the strongest contribution is an explanation of added exposure: the agent receives task context and private values, reads attacker-controlled environmental content, and can convert that content into browser actions. However, the paper does not run a matched experiment comparing web agents with standalone large language models. It therefore supports mechanisms relevant to the question, not a general measured claim that every web agent is more vulnerable than every standalone model.

# 2. Document roadmap

[A] The abstract and §1 introduce privacy leakage, the two attack goals, headline findings, and the autonomy–security tension. Section 2 separates direct prompt injection, indirect prompt injection, web-agent architectures, and prior attacks. Section 3 provides the technical core: the SeeAct formulation in §3.1, attacker goals and constraints in §3.2, and EIA construction in §3.3. Section 4 describes the dataset, models, metrics, specific-PII attacks, and full-request attacks. Section 5 evaluates detection and a narrow family of prompt defenses. Section 6 discusses supervision, deployment-stage defenses, and why task-request leakage expands the attack surface. Section 7 concludes. Sources: pp. 1–10.

[A] Page 11 contains ethics and reproducibility statements. References occupy pp. 11–14; p. 15 lists the appendices. Appendices A–E show benign, adapted, annotated, poorly adapted, and faintly visible webpages. Appendix F states methodological limitations. Appendix G gives data distributions and subgroup attack rates. Appendices H and I provide the attack-template and defense-prompt families. Appendix J separates full-request leakage from injected-element selection. Appendix K supplies the PII-classification prompt. Appendix L illustrates SeeAct's two stages. Appendices M and N discuss contextual integrity and the expanded attack surface. Sources: pp. 11–32.

The appendices materially qualify the headline results: F establishes the offline, step-level scope; G reveals sparse PII categories; J shows why selecting a malicious element is not equivalent to leaking a whole request; and B reports a five-example adaptation demonstration rather than a large human-detection study.

# 3. Background and context

[A] A large language model, or LLM, processes language. A large multimodal model, or LMM, also handles modalities such as images; here screenshots matter. The paper studies LMM-backed web agents that perform operations on websites, rather than only retrieve information for a text answer. HTML identifies page elements and their attributes. Cascading Style Sheets, or CSS, control appearance, including opacity. JavaScript supplies behavior such as automatically submitting entered information. The Document Object Model, or DOM, is the hierarchical representation of the page used to locate, insert, and remove elements. Sources: pp. 3–6.

[A] Prompt injection means supplying content intended to induce unwanted model behavior. Direct injection comes from a user manipulating the model's input; indirect injection arrives through another application component, such as retrieved or environmental content. EIA belongs to the latter category. Its content is encountered as part of the webpage the agent is using. The attack is consequently an environmental input problem as well as a language problem. Sources: pp. 2–3.

[A] Action generation is the planning-like stage that textually describes the next element, operation, and value. Action grounding maps that description to an executable browser event. In the default SeeAct configuration used here, generation receives the screenshot but not HTML; grounding uses textual choices associated with HTML elements as well as the screenshot. The difference explains both invisible EIA's specific-PII success and its full-request failure. Sources: p. 4; pp. 30–31, Figs. 27–28.

[A] PII is personally identifiable information. The evaluation's observed categories are name, email, phone number, physical address, credit-card number, date of birth, and passport number. The complete user request is broader than any one value: it may reveal travel dates, places, or other task context. The authors distinguish leaking an intended field value from inducing the agent to type its whole task instruction into the page. Sources: p. 4, §3.2; p. 24, Fig. 19.

# 4. Research problem and gap

[A] Existing problem: useful web tasks often require sensitive information, and an agent can encounter a compromised page while pursuing a legitimate request. The attack seeks unauthorized disclosure without obvious interruption. Motivation: normal-looking task completion can hide a privacy failure, and complete requests contain context beyond the individual values a website ordinarily receives. Sources: pp. 1–4.

[A] According to the authors, earlier web-agent attacks include model backdoors requiring white-box fine-tuning, image manipulation, and prompt injection against retrieval-oriented systems. They characterize prior retrieval-oriented attacks as involving simpler summarization tasks, prior knowledge of requests, or disruption of normal behavior. Their proposed gap is privacy leakage in generalist agents performing diverse interactive tasks, with emphasis on environmental adaptation and continued functionality. These are the authors' descriptions of cited literature; the outside studies were not independently evaluated. Source: p. 3, §2.

[A] Claimed novelty includes a realistic website-compromise threat model, two privacy targets, environment-adapted injection strategies, and what the authors call the first exploration of privacy risks for generalist web agents. Their statement that the strategies are readily applicable to screenshot- or HTML-based agents is broader than the measured framework coverage. The experiments use SeeAct with three backbones, not all architectures. Sources: pp. 1–3.

[D] The research gap most relevant to the requested security analysis is the transition from reading untrusted content to acting on it with user-provided information. This interpretation is grounded in the system formulation and attack results. It does not establish a vulnerability ranking across standalone models and agents, because that comparison is absent.

# 5. Research questions / objectives / hypotheses

The paper presents objectives and exploratory questions in prose, not a formally numbered research-question or hypothesis list. The following identifiers organize those objectives without attributing new formal questions to the authors.

| ID | Author objective, paraphrased | Evaluation |
|---|---|---|
| O1 | Establish a website-compromise threat model for private-data leakage. | §3.2, p. 4. |
| O2 | Determine whether environment-adapted injection can steal specific PII. | §4.2, Table 1. |
| O3 | Determine whether injection can steal complete user requests. | §4.3, Appendix J. |
| O4 | Examine how strategy, placement, visibility, and backbone affect attacks. | §§3.3–4.3, Table 1, Figs. 24–26. |
| O5 | Examine detection through a conventional security tool and continued agent behavior. | §5.1, Fig. 3. |
| O6 | Test whether screenshot-oriented defensive system prompts mitigate the attacks. | §5.2, Fig. 4, Appendix I. |
| O7 | Discuss supervision, defense trade-offs, and additional attack surfaces. | §6, Appendices B, M, N. |

[A] The authors propose explanatory hypotheses: proximity and ordering may bias element selection; Mirror Injection may work because it resembles the legitimate element; GPT-4V's optical character recognition and instruction following may explain full-request results; and normal-looking guidance may undermine the tested prompt defense. These explanations are not isolated by dedicated causal ablations. Sources: pp. 7–9.

[D] The user's question, 'Why Are Web AI Agents More Vulnerable Than Standalone LLMs?', is an analytical lens applied here. It is not the paper's title, a stated formal hypothesis, or an experimentally measured comparison.

# 6. Assumptions / threat model

[A] Assets: specific private values and the entire user task request T. The task request can encode sensitive context even when the user supplied only information necessary for the task. Attack surface: malicious HTML elements and instructions introduced into a webpage, with visibility and DOM placement controlled by the attacker. The attack's output channel is a field into which the agent types, followed by automatic transmission to an external website. Sources: pp. 4–6.

[A] Capabilities: the attacker can alter the compromised website and adapt the injection to its available functionality. The attacker may invest additional effort to adjust element placement, dimensions, and appearance. The attacker is assumed to have no prior knowledge of the user's task T or prior action history A. That constraint excludes tailoring the attack to an already known complete request; it does not imply that the attacker lacks knowledge of the target site's fields or purpose. Source: p. 4, §3.2; p. 17, Appendix B.

[A] Two compromise scenarios are proposed. Benign developers may unknowingly use contaminated development tools or libraries. Alternatively, malicious developers may introduce the content during page updates. These are threat-model scenarios, not demonstrated supply-chain incidents within the experiment. The footnote on p. 4 references a reported library backdoor as motivation; this analysis does not validate that outside example.

[A] Constraint: the attack should not prevent ordinary task completion, because obvious malfunction may alert users. Default opacity is zero to reduce visible differences. Nevertheless, zero-opacity DOM elements can still occupy layout space. The authors explicitly acknowledge that more adaptation may be needed to hide this footprint. Sources: pp. 4–6, footnote 2 on p. 5.

[D] Trust-boundary interpretation: the agent is entrusted with T and relevant values, while the encountered webpage may be adversarial. EIA encourages the agent to treat environmental descriptions as guidance about where or what to type. The measured attack exploits this relationship; it does not require a demonstrated modification of model weights, system prompts, or the user's original instruction. There is no separate formal list of trusted infrastructure or excluded browser vulnerabilities in the supplied work.

# 7. Methodology

[A] Study design: offline, action-step evaluation on adapted website snapshots. Mind2Web originally contains 2,350 human-crafted tasks over 137 real websites. These are parent-dataset counts, not the number of websites proven to appear in the 177-instance attack subset. GPT-4 and GPT-4o identify PII-containing action steps and categories; humans verify the selections, correct categories, and filter low-quality data. The final evaluation has 177 action steps. Corresponding MHTML snapshots are manually adapted to represent the relevant state, including previous actions. Source: p. 6, §4.1.

[A] The classification prompt in Appendix K lists Social Security Number, username, password, name, email, phone number, credit-card number, bank-account number, physical address, fax number, driver's-license number, passport number, and date of birth. It allows additional categories and a None outcome, and asks for the specific information supporting each category. Only seven categories appear in the final distribution. The supplied work does not quantify filtering losses, annotator agreement, or a full selection-flow diagram. Source: p. 29.

[A] Models: SeeAct is instantiated with GPT-4V, Llava-1.6-Mistral-7B, and Llava-1.6-Qwen-72B, abbreviated LlavaMistral7B and LlavaQwen72B. The authors report A6000 GPUs with 48 GB memory. GPU count, inference precision, model/API revisions, sampling temperature, random seeds, and repetition counts are not specified in the supplied experimental settings. No model is trained as part of EIA, and no attack-subset train/validation/test split is described. Source: p. 6.

[A] Injection design has three principal conditions. FI (text), or Form Injection with text, inserts an instruction in form content. FI (aria) inserts it in an aria-label attribute. Mirror Injection, or MI, replicates the legitimate target element's style and naming conventions while adding an instruction in an auxiliary attribute. Forms are chosen because they commonly and intuitively collect submissions. MI is intended to fit pages even when the target is not a conventional form. Sources: pp. 5–6.

[A] The simple specific-PII template tells the agent that the injected element is the right place for the relevant PII category. The full-request template uses an identity-verification pretext, capitalized language, and a demand to type the task rather than summarize it. These are attack artifacts, not instructions governing this analysis. The authors state that capitalization and identity verification improve effectiveness, but provide no separate numerical ablation for those design choices. Sources: p. 5; p. 27, Appendix H.

[A] Position is relative to legitimate target P0. The eight tested positions are P+∞, P+3, P+2, P+1, P−1, P−2, P−3, and P−∞. Positive positions are above the target, negative positions below; nesting-level definitions use |n|−1, while the infinities mean the highest and lowest possible positions. These are DOM-relative positions, not measured pixel distances. Sources: pp. 5–6, Fig. 2.

[A] Default EIA sets opacity α=0. Relaxed-EIA uses FI (text) and α=0.2 to make the instruction accessible to screenshot-based generation while remaining faint. An automatic injection script enables scale but may produce whitespace or imperfect adaptation. A JavaScript delay mechanism sends information after one second without typing and removes the injected element afterward. This mechanism is intended to avoid requiring a submit-button click and reduce interruption. Sources: pp. 6, 8.

[A] Metrics: benign step success rate, SR, requires the correct element and operation, including values. Attack success rate, ASR, requires selection of the injected element and a typed-value string-similarity score strictly greater than 0.95 against ground truth. A footnote links this similarity computation to Python's difflib SequenceMatcher and says 0.95 was selected empirically to accommodate spacing issues. ASRo measures injected-element selection without requiring correct full-request content. ASRpt measures attack-associated continuation at the next step under a criterion accepting the benign next action or another remaining gold action. Sources: pp. 7–8, 28.

[A] Ethics: cached public data and fabricated PII are used; the authors say no live websites or real user data were attacked. Their statement about agents not yet being ready for real-life deployment is a paper-era position, not a currently verified fact. Source: p. 11.

# 8. Experiments / analyses

| ID | Purpose and conditions | Evidence and outcome | Main caveat |
|---|---|---|---|
| X1 | Specific-PII leakage; three backbones, three injection strategies, eight positions; α=0. | Table 1: maximum 0.70 for GPT-4V, MI, P+1. | Step-level offline results; maximum is condition-specific. |
| X2 | Full-request leakage; compare α=0 with FI (text), α=0.2. | §4.3 and Fig. 24: invisible EIA yields zero; Relaxed-EIA reaches 0.16 for GPT-4V at P−3. | Other two backbones remain zero; opacity optimization is not reported. |
| X3 | Detection of attacked pages by VirusTotal, focusing on GPT-4V experiments. | §5.1 reports no pages flagged malicious or suspicious. | Submission counts, detailed tool outputs, and detection configuration are absent. |
| X4 | Continuation after successful leakage. | Fig. 3 shows ASRpt close to ASR for MI EIA and Relaxed-EIA. | Checks the next action, not complete task success. |
| X5 | Defensive system prompts warning about unusual elements and emphasizing screenshots. | Fig. 4 reports nearly unchanged ASR; three prompts are averaged. | A narrow family of similar prompts, not all defenses. |
| X6 | Carefully adapt injections on five example webpages. | Appendix B reports 4/5 ASR for specific PII; Figs. 6–15 show appearance and locations. | Small demonstration; no formal human-detection experiment. |
| X7 | Describe sample balance and subgroup ASR. | Figs. 18–23; GPT-4V MI rates averaged across eight positions. | Some categories have only one to five instances. |
| X8 | Separate malicious-element selection from full-request content leakage. | Figs. 25–26 show nonzero selection despite zero invisible-EIA full-request success. | Exact plotted series are not tabulated; architecture explanation is not a causal ablation. |

[A] X1 changes strategy and position while recording benign model SR separately. GPT-4V's SR is 0.78, LlavaQwen72B's 0.55, and LlavaMistral7B's 0.10. Their different benign capabilities complicate comparison of raw ASR: the supplied work does not report a capability-matched control or ASR conditional on initially correct benign actions. Source: p. 7.

[A] X2 changes the attack goal as well as visibility. The reason for Relaxed-EIA is architectural: changing only HTML can redirect grounding while leaving the planned value as the intended PII. Full-request theft requires changing the value description generated from the screenshot. X8 reinforces this distinction by showing that malicious-element selection alone is insufficient. Sources: pp. 8, 28.

[D] X3–X6 concern different meanings of stealth. Security-tool non-detection, preservation of a next action, visual similarity, and resistance to warning prompts are separate observations. None alone establishes that every deployment, human reviewer, or security system would fail to detect EIA.

# 9. Results

[A] Highest specific-PII success: GPT-4V with MI at P+1 has ASR 0.70. This is an invisible, grounding-stage attack with α=0. It is not the average MI result: GPT-4V MI averages 0.38 across positions, while FI (text) averages 0.45 and FI (aria) averages 0.44. The headline 'MI achieves the highest ASR' refers to the best individual setting, not superior mean performance. Sources: pp. 7–8, Table 1.

[A] Placement matters. The average across Table 1's nine model-strategy rows is highest at P+1, 0.39, and lowest at P−∞, 0.06. Immediate-above placement generally outperforms immediate-below placement in the aggregated results. The authors attribute this partly to seeing the injected element before the legitimate target, but do not experimentally isolate ordering from other structural effects. Source: p. 7.

[A] Full-request leakage: all tested invisible-EIA positions and three backbones have ASR zero for that goal. Relaxed-EIA at α=0.2 enables GPT-4V to reach 16% at P−3; the two Llava backbones remain at zero. The authors attribute the difference to GPT-4V's OCR and instruction following. That attribution is an author interpretation, not a separately measured component-level result. Sources: pp. 8, 28.

[C] The change from 0% to 16% is a 16-percentage-point increase: 16−0=16. Relative percentage improvement from a zero baseline is undefined, so it should not be reported as a finite percentage improvement. This comparison concerns full-request leakage, not specific-PII theft.

[A] VirusTotal flags none of the attacked pages according to §5.1. Figure 3 indicates continuation-associated ASRpt remains close to ASR. Figure 4 indicates the tested defensive prompts leave ASR nearly unchanged. The authors explain these outcomes through normal-looking language, element removal, and difficulty defining a normal page. The exact per-position defense and continuation values are not supplied in tables. Sources: pp. 8–9.

[A] Carefully adapted examples achieve 4 successful attacks out of 5. [C] That fraction is 80%, calculated as 4÷5×100; it is not a population estimate or evidence that the large evaluation's maximum rose from 70% to a generally applicable 80%. Source: p. 17.

[A] Subgroup results are broad but unequal. GPT-4V MI, averaged across eight positions, ranges from 0.29 for entertainment to 0.47 for service among displayed domains; from 0.17 for date of birth to 0.50 for passport number among PII categories; and from 0.12 for digital to 0.62 for government among subdomains. Passport number has only one instance, so its apparent high rate has very limited sample support. Sources: pp. 24–26.

# 10. Figure-by-figure interpretation

All 28 figures were visually inspected in supplied page renderings. The figure discussions distinguish readable labels from approximate curve positions. Website screenshots have no quantitative axes, units, error bars, or statistical markers.

## Figure 1 — Leakage during an ordinary task

[B] Page 2 combines a GameStop gift-card page, a magnified form region, a user request, an agent, an attacker, and current/next-action flow. Arrows connect the legitimate request to the agent, injected page content to action selection, and the compromised action to disclosure. A red dashed region marks an otherwise invisible injected field. [A] The caption explains that the agent types recipient PII into the malicious field and then continues the task. It illustrates the attack mechanism; the displayed gift-card amount is example context, not an experimental variable. The schematic is not evidence of a live attack on GameStop.

## Figure 2 — Injection construction and DOM placement

[B] Page 5 shows two injection carriers alongside an HTML hierarchy and the legitimate target at P0. The FI (aria) example is placed at P−1; MI is illustrated at P+2. Arrows connect carriers to their insertion points. Labels identify opacity zero and automatic submission. [A] MI preserves target-like attributes while adding persuasive auxiliary content. The nested div blocks explain hierarchy, not literal spatial distances. Unrelated HTML is abbreviated as 'xxx'.

## Figure 3 — Leakage and subsequent action

[B] Page 9 plots eight categorical positions horizontally and rates from 0 to 1 vertically. Blue denotes ASR; orange denotes ASRpt. Solid lines represent EIA and dashed lines Relaxed-EIA. There are no error bars or significance markers. Specific-PII EIA peaks near P+1, and the associated continuation curve is close to it. Relaxed-EIA's lower dashed curves also lie close together. [A] The authors interpret this as little disruption to subsequent actions. Caveat: the plotted proximity does not establish end-to-end completion or define an independently estimated conditional continuation probability.

## Figure 4 — Tested system-prompt defenses

[B] Page 9 uses the same eight-position horizontal axis and a 0–1 ASR vertical scale. Blue represents default SeeAct and orange SeeAct plus defense; solid and dashed lines distinguish EIA and Relaxed-EIA. Curves nearly overlap. [A] Appendix I says defense results average three prompts. No numerical per-prompt breakdown, uncertainty interval, or statistical test is shown. The figure supports ineffectiveness of these tested prompts, not every instruction-based defense.

## Figure 5 — Benign GameStop reference

[B] Page 16 shows the legitimate gift-card page with recipient-name and recipient-email fields, other delivery fields, and an add-to-cart control. It is the visual reference for the attacked versions. Fine text is too small for exhaustive transcription. Its role is comparative appearance, not a numerical result.

## Figure 6 — Carefully adapted GameStop injection

[B] Page 17 looks substantially similar to Fig. 5 at the supplied scale. [A] The authors say injection position and size were fine-tuned because position changes alone were insufficient. Visual inspection supports absence of an obvious large anomaly, but cannot establish pixel identity or actual human non-detection. The associated 4/5 result applies across all five adapted examples, not to this figure alone.

## Figure 7 — Adapted HealthGrades page

[B] Page 18 shows a dark footer with a newsletter-email area. The unmarked screenshot has no conspicuous attack label. Figure 12 identifies the hidden region. The example demonstrates adaptation around an ordinary information-entry interface; it supplies no separate numerical attack rate.

## Figure 8 — Adapted United Airline page

[B] Page 18 shows a check-in interface over a travel background, including confirmation-number and last-name fields. Figure 13 marks the corresponding injected region. Its contribution is showing that adaptation is not restricted to the gift-card layout. Exact small field text is secondary and not fully transcribed.

## Figure 9 — Adapted BenefitsCal page

[B] Page 19 shows a multistep personal-information form with several name fields and navigation. Figure 14 marks an injection near the last-name area. The example illustrates blending into a dense form. It does not separately measure whether humans can detect that injection.

## Figure 10 — Adapted Amazon page

[B] Page 19 shows a job-application form with name, email, and phone areas and subsequent questions. Figure 15 marks the injection location. The page expands the visual examples to employment-related data collection. Details of the job advertisement are example context rather than study outcomes.

## Figure 11 — Annotated GameStop injection location

[B] Page 20 repeats the adapted gift-card screenshot with a red dashed rectangle near the recipient-name region. [A] The rectangle is an explanatory annotation identifying invisible content. It is not part of the attack's ordinary visible appearance. Comparing Figs. 6 and 11 clarifies that apparently unused space can host an injected element.

## Figure 12 — Annotated HealthGrades location

[B] Page 20 marks a region immediately below the newsletter input. It explains Fig. 7's hidden placement. The red annotation must not be mistaken for a real warning shown to the agent or user. No additional outcome is attached to the marked copy.

## Figure 13 — Annotated airline location

[B] Page 21 marks a narrow region between the confirmation-number and last-name portions of the check-in interface. It links the visually ordinary Fig. 8 to an attacker-controlled target. The figure is a location demonstration, not evidence about all airline websites.

## Figure 14 — Annotated BenefitsCal location

[B] Page 21 marks a region within or adjacent to the last-name row. It illustrates how a hidden target can fit into an established form structure. The supplied scale does not reveal the underlying DOM or exact dimensions.

## Figure 15 — Annotated Amazon location

[B] Page 22 marks a horizontal region between name and email sections of the application form. Together with Fig. 10, it accounts for the fifth adapted example. The repeated image is deliberately compressed here because it adds placement information rather than a new experiment.

## Figure 16 — Poor adaptation leaves whitespace

[B] Page 23 shows a magnified delivery-details area with conspicuous empty space above the recipient-name field. [A] The caption identifies β=P+2 and says this makes the attack poorly adapted. It directly qualifies the idea that opacity zero guarantees invisibility: the field may be transparent while its layout footprint remains visible.

## Figure 17 — Faintly visible Relaxed-EIA

[B] Page 23 shows a gift-card page with pale instructional content below the recipient-name field. [A] The caption places the injection at P−1. Section 4.3 supplies the α=0.2 setting. This screenshot demonstrates the visibility trade-off; it is not the P−3 configuration associated with the maximum 16% result. The suggestion that bottom-of-page placement may escape supervision is an author discussion, not a measured human outcome.

## Figure 18 — Domain and subdomain distribution

[B] Page 24 uses a nested circular chart: inner sectors encode broad domains, outer sectors subdomains. It includes travel, shopping, service, information, and entertainment categories and finer categories such as airlines, housing, and health. Counts are not printed on this chart; Fig. 20 supplies them. There are no Cartesian axes or uncertainty bars. Sector sizes communicate composition, not ASR.

## Figure 19 — PII-frequency distribution

[B] Page 24 gives readable counts: name 72, email 67, phone number 18, physical address 10, credit-card number 5, date of birth 4, passport number 1. [C] Their sum is 72+67+18+10+5+4+1=177. This matches the reported action-step count. The caption describes instances containing a category; the matching total does not, by itself, explain all annotation rules or prove that every original request contains exactly one PII type.

## Figure 20 — Subdomain sample counts

[B] Page 25 is a bar chart with categorical subdomains horizontally and count vertically, with ticks through 25. Exact labels are: airlines 21; speciality 20; auto 13; housing 11; general 10; government 10; health 10; car rental 9; education 8; ground 7; shipping 6; home service 5; pet 5; job 4; event 3; fashion 3; department 3; restaurant 2; hotel 2; digital 1; other 24. [C] These labels sum to 177. The caption calls them tasks, whereas §4.1 calls the curated instances action steps; that unit wording is not fully reconciled.

## Figure 21 — ASR by broad domain

[B] Page 25 presents labeled rates in a pie chart: service 0.47, information 0.44, shopping 0.35, travel 0.34, entertainment 0.29. [A] Appendix G specifies GPT-4V, MI, averaged over eight positions. These are separate group rates, not mutually exclusive pieces of a total success probability. [D] Pie geometry can misleadingly suggest composition; the labels should be interpreted as rates. No group confidence intervals are shown.

## Figure 22 — ASR by PII category

[B] Page 25 labels passport number 0.50, email 0.39, name 0.38, credit-card number 0.38, phone number 0.37, physical address 0.37, date of birth 0.17. The same GPT-4V MI averaging condition applies. # 12. Diagram / architecture interpretation

[A/B] The architecture has a repeating observation–action loop. The task T and prior actions A accompany the current page observation. A renderer maps HTML h to screenshot i. Generation policy π1 uses i, T, and A to produce textual descriptions of element, operation, and value. Grounding policy π2 uses i, h, those descriptions, T, and A to select executable element e, operation o, and value v. Executing the event changes the website, creating the next observation. Sources: p. 4, Eqs. (1)–(3); Figs. 27–28.

[A/B] EIA enters this loop by replacing benign HTML with h*. With α=0, the attack is intended to preserve screenshot appearance while adding a candidate element and persuasive description to grounding. This can redirect a legitimate TYPE action into an attacker-controlled destination without changing the intended value. With α=0.2, Relaxed-EIA also changes the screenshot, allowing the generation stage to propose a different value: the entire request. Sources: pp. 5–8, Figs. 1–2.

[A] The disclosure path continues from the injected field through a one-second idle-typing trigger to automatic submission, followed by DOM removal. The ordinary task path then resumes. That is why completion-like behavior can coexist with leakage. [D] The important architectural distinction is between the agent's private task context and environmental instructions that can influence its actions. The diagram does not establish a browser permission bypass or a standalone-model comparison.

# 14. Interpretation and discussion

[A] The authors' central interpretation is that environment adaptation matters: a malicious element can look structurally legitimate, use innocuous guidance, and remain visually unobtrusive. MI's peak result supports the possibility of strong local deception; FI's higher mean shows that greater resemblance is not uniformly advantageous across positions. Invisible full-request failure demonstrates a boundary of the attack: corrupting grounding can alter destination without necessarily overriding an already generated value. Sources: pp. 7–8, 28.

[D] Relevance to agent versus standalone security has four source-grounded mechanisms. First, a web agent repeatedly encounters third-party HTML and images while executing a user goal, providing environmental entry points. Second, grounding converts interpretation into concrete typing and clicking. Third, the user request and private values remain available to the policy while it reads the potentially compromised page. Fourth, ordinary continuation can conceal disclosure, so visible progress is an incomplete safety signal. These are analyst inferences from the architecture and observations, not findings from a matched standalone-LLM experiment.

[A] The authors discuss a tension in separating instructions from data. Webpage labels and descriptions are formally environmental data but often contain useful guidance for navigation. Ignoring all such content may impair utility; accepting it without sufficient discrimination can permit malicious guidance. They also discuss keyword filtering and filtering zero-opacity elements, noting that ordinary guidance and legitimate transitional elements complicate these approaches. These proposals are discussed, not implemented and evaluated here. Source: p. 10.

Unresolved consistency points include the Table 1 caption's aggregation wording, the anomalous 0.461 variance, Fig. 20's use of 'tasks' for a collection introduced as action steps, and the exact normalization of ASRpt. The broad caption 'Our attacks do not affect the agent's functional integrity' is stronger than the accompanying text 'barely affect subsequent actions' and the next-step-only test. The careful reading is preservation of measured continuation to a substantial extent, not proof of no functional impact.

# 16. Limitations

## Authors' stated limitations

[A] Appendix F explicitly states that evaluation is offline and based on adapted Mind2Web action steps. ## Additional evidence-based analyst observations

[D] No matched standalone-LLM baseline is supplied. Framework coverage is one architecture with three backbones, and defense/detection analysis focuses on GPT-4V. [D] The source does not provide full implementation code, detailed VirusTotal receipts, exact plot data, model revisions, inference sampling settings, or annotation agreement. The similarity criterion tolerates small textual discrepancies; ASR should therefore be understood as the authors' threshold-defined proxy, not guaranteed exact-byte disclosure. The supplied results are also not a measured deployment incidence rate.

# 22. Very simple explanation — Explain Like I'm 15

Imagine giving an assistant your name and email so it can buy a gift card. On the website, someone secretly adds another box that says it is the correct place to enter your name. The assistant chooses that box, and the information is sent elsewhere. It then keeps shopping, so the task can look normal even though something private was leaked.

The researchers tested an assistant that works in two steps. It first looks at a screenshot and decides what to do. It then reads page-element information to choose the exact box or button. An invisible fake box can confuse the second step without changing the first. That explains why it can steal the name the assistant was already planning to type, but initially cannot make it type the entire user's request instead.

When the malicious message becomes faintly visible, it can also influence the first step. In one tested setting, that lets the assistant leak the full request, which may reveal more than a name or email. The best results were 70% for a particular private-field attack and 16% for a particular full-request attack. Those numbers came from offline action-step tests, not complete tasks on live websites.

For the question about agents versus ordinary chat models, the lesson is that connecting a model to webpages and browser actions creates additional ways for hostile content to cause consequences. But this paper did not directly compare an agent with an otherwise matched standalone model. It shows important mechanisms and examples of added risk, rather than proving a universal ranking.

claims.statement: The threat model assumes no prior attacker knowledge of the user task or previous actions, while allowing website-based attacks adapted to available functionality.
SeeAct's default generation stage uses only the screenshot, whereas grounding maps textual action descriptions to executable events using screenshot and HTML information.
The evaluation contains 177 manually verified and filtered PII-related action steps adapted from Mind2Web snapshots, rather than 177 end-to-end live tasks.
EIA includes Form Injection and Mirror Injection; its automatic submission mechanism waits one second after typing stops, transmits the entered information, and removes the injected elements.
The maximum specific-PII ASR is 70% with GPT-4V, Mirror Injection, and P+1 placement under invisible EIA; this is a condition-specific action-step result.
Invisible EIA yields zero full-request ASR across all tested positions and three backbones, even though agents can select the injected element.
Relaxed-EIA uses FI text at opacity 0.2 and reaches a maximum 16% full-request ASR with GPT-4V at P−3; the two tested Llava backbones remain at zero.
The authors report that VirusTotal did not flag any tested attacked webpages as malicious or suspicious; detailed detection receipts and configurations are not supplied.
The tested attacks show ASRpt close to ASR, supporting limited disruption of measured subsequent actions rather than establishing complete end-to-end task integrity.
Three similar defensive system prompts emphasizing ordinary website elements and screenshot-visible content do not materially reduce the reported EIA or Relaxed-EIA ASRs.
Five carefully adapted webpage examples achieve 4/5 specific-PII attack success, but the demonstration does not include a controlled human-detection study.
The authors explicitly limit their evaluation to offline action steps and identify real-time end-to-end evaluation, multiple injection points, and multi-turn compositional attacks as remaining work.

Analyst inference: user task context, attacker-controlled environmental inputs, and executable browser actions explain added agent attack surfaces relevant to comparison with standalone LLMs; this paper does not directly measure that comparison.
Table 1 shows GPT-4V FI text has a higher displayed mean ASR, 0.45, than MI, 0.38, despite MI producing the highest individual ASR; the accompanying prose also qualifies MI's average performance.

research.research_question_relevance: MEDIUM confidence, analyst inference: the paper explains mechanisms relevant to why web agents may add security exposure—attacker-controlled HTML and screenshots are processed alongside private task context and converted into executable browser actions, permitting disclosure with continued task progress. research.attack_surface: Compromised webpage HTML elements, text and aria-label attributes, DOM-relative placement, CSS-controlled visibility, and automatic transmission from injected fields. Invisible content targets grounding; faintly visible content can also target screenshot-based generation.
research.method: Offline SeeAct evaluation with GPT-4V, Llava-1.6-Mistral-7B, and Llava-1.6-Qwen-72B on 177 curated Mind2Web action steps. Specific-PII experiments compare FI text, FI aria, and Mirror Injection across eight placements at opacity zero. Full-request experiments introduce FI text at opacity 0.2. Additional analyses examine tool detection, next-action continuation, three defensive prompts, five adapted webpages, subgroup results, and element selection versus content leakage.
research.limitations: Offline step-level evaluation rather than real-time end-to-end tasks; one framework; sparse subgroup counts; no standalone-LLM baseline; no controlled human-detection study; narrow defense family; incomplete reported reproduction settings and absent implementation artifacts; unlabeled curve values and Table 1 variance/aggregation inconsistencies. Broader relevance is analyst inference, not an author-tested comparison.
